_source: Taxonomy validated against WoRMS REST API on 2026-09-29; husbandry curated from widely published reef-keeping guidance; not FishBase
_notes: IDs are not stored here; scripts/add-reef-batch.mjs assigns them from 200001 in list order. aphiaId and family are the WoRMS accepted record. careDefaults apply to every entry unless the entry overrides tempRangeCelsius or phRange. maxLengthCm is null for corals, where colony or disc size is not a body length. soldAs lists older trade names that the add script also checks against the catalog.

corals.note: A short-branched, colorful Acropora for a stable, mature reef with strong light and flow.
corals.comments: Small-polyp stony coral that needs very stable alkalinity, calcium and magnesium, low but non-zero nutrients, and intense light. Sensitive to parameter swings; best added once a tank has been stable for many months.

corals.note: A plating montipora that grows in swirling shelves; a common first SPS.
corals.comments: Forms thin whorled plates that can shade corals beneath them as they grow. More forgiving than Acropora but still needs stable alkalinity and calcium. Watch for montipora-eating nudibranchs on new frags.

corals.note: A fast-growing branching montipora that is one of the hardier SPS corals.
corals.comments: Branching small-polyp stony coral that tolerates a wider range of light than most SPS. Grows quickly once settled and is often used to learn stony-coral dosing.

corals.note: Thin, pointed branches that form a dense nest; pink and green forms are common.
corals.comments: Delicate branching SPS that needs strong light and flow and stable water. Branches are brittle and it can be quickly stung by neighbors, so give it space.

corals.note: A blunt-branched SPS that is widely aquacultured and relatively forgiving.
corals.comments: Branching small-polyp stony coral with thick, rounded branch tips. Tolerates moderate light and grows steadily with good flow and stable alkalinity.

corals.note: A fast-growing branching SPS that can seed new colonies around the tank.
corals.comments: Hardy for an SPS and one of the few corals that often releases planula larvae in aquariums, so new colonies can appear on the rockwork.

corals.note: Long flowing tentacles with bright tips; a favorite host for clownfish.
corals.comments: Large-polyp stony coral with long sweeper tentacles that sting nearby corals; leave at least 15 cm of space around it. Prefers moderate, alternating flow that moves the tentacles without tearing them.

corals.taxonomyNote: Sold as Euphyllia ancora. WoRMS lists Euphyllia ancora (AphiaID 207614) as a superseded combination; the accepted name is Fimbriaphyllia ancora.
corals.note: Hammer- or anchor-shaped tentacle tips that sway in moderate flow.
corals.comments: Large-polyp stony coral with stinging sweeper tentacles; give it room from other corals. Wall and branching forms are both common in the trade.

corals.note: Big green polyps on branching tubes that eagerly take food.
corals.comments: Hardy large-polyp stony coral that responds well to regular target feeding with small meaty foods. Grows by adding new heads on tube-like branches.

corals.taxonomyNote: Plate corals are sold at genus level as Fungia; Fungia fungites, the type species, is used here.
corals.note: A free-living disc coral that sits on the sand and can move slowly.
corals.comments: Solitary, free-living stony coral kept on the sand bed, not the rockwork. Tentacles extend and can sting neighbors; avoid placing it where it can wander into other corals.

corals.note: A fleshy, often fluorescent brain coral that sits on the sand.
corals.comments: Free-living large-polyp stony coral kept on the sand bed. Inflates its tissue in low flow and extends feeding tentacles at night; target feed small meaty foods.

corals.taxonomyNote: Long sold as Acanthastrea lordhowensis; the accepted WoRMS name is Micromussa lordhowensis.
corals.note: Fleshy, multicolored polyps that are collected for their color morphs.
corals.comments: Encrusting large-polyp stony coral that grows well under modest light when target fed. Extends short sweeper tentacles at night, so leave a little space around it.

corals.note: Striped tube-shaped heads that branch and grow into a bouquet.
corals.comments: Hardy large-polyp stony coral and a common first LPS. Extends short sweepers at night; accepts small meaty foods and grows new heads steadily.

corals.note: Fleshy, inflated polyps in red, pink, and green; happy in shaded spots.
corals.comments: Large-polyp stony coral that prefers low light and gentle flow. Polyps inflate strongly when conditions suit it; small meaty foods help growth.

corals.taxonomyNote: Leather corals are sold at genus level as Sarcophyton; Sarcophyton glaucum is used here as a well-known accepted species.
corals.note: A mushroom-shaped leather coral with a cap of long polyps.
corals.comments: Hardy soft coral that releases chemical compounds (terpenes) that can irritate nearby stony corals; activated carbon helps in mixed reefs. Periodically sheds a waxy film and stays closed for a few days.

corals.taxonomyNote: Sold as Sinularia flexibilis. WoRMS lists Sinularia flexibilis (AphiaID 288521) as a superseded combination; the accepted name is Sclerophytum flexibile. The hobby genus-level name is Sinularia.
corals.note: Soft, swaying fingers that move gracefully in the current.
corals.comments: Hardy soft coral that grows quickly and propagates easily. Like other leathers it can release chemicals that affect stony corals; run carbon in mixed reefs.

corals.taxonomyNote: Pulsing corals are sold as Xenia or Heteroxenia; Xenia umbellata is used here as a well-known accepted species.
corals.note: Feathery polyps that open and close in a rhythmic pulse.
corals.comments: Soft coral that spreads rapidly across rock and can overgrow slower corals. Easiest to control on an isolated rock. Growth and pulsing vary between tanks.

corals.taxonomyNote: Clove polyps are sold at genus level as Clavularia; Clavularia viridis is used here as a well-known accepted species.
corals.note: Eight-armed feathery polyps that spread across rock on runners.
corals.comments: Hardy soft coral that spreads by stolons and can cover rock quickly. A good beginner coral; place it where spreading will not crowd other corals.

corals.taxonomyNote: Often sold as Pachyclavularia violacea, which WoRMS lists as a superseded combination (AphiaID 1346552) of Briareum violaceum. Taxonomically an encrusting briareid; treated as a soft coral in the hobby.
corals.note: A glowing green carpet of polyps on a purple mat.
corals.comments: Very hardy and fast-spreading encrusting coral that can overgrow rock, glass, and other corals. Many keepers grow it on an isolated rock to keep it in check.

corals.taxonomyNote: Zoanthids are sold by color-morph trade names at genus level (Zoanthus); Zoanthus sociatus is used here as a well-known accepted species. WoRMS also holds a homonym record (AphiaID 869585, taxon inquirendum); the accepted record is used.
corals.note: Colonies of small colorful polyps, collected in endless named color morphs.
corals.comments: Hardy colonial zoanthid that spreads across rock. Some zoanthids contain palytoxin: wear gloves and eye protection when handling or fragging, and never boil rock with them attached.

corals.taxonomyNote: Palys are sold at genus level as Palythoa; Palythoa grandis is used here as a well-known accepted species.
corals.note: Larger polyps than Zoanthus that grow quickly and eat more readily.
corals.comments: Hardy colonial zoanthid. Palythoa species can contain high levels of palytoxin, a dangerous toxin: wear gloves and eye protection when handling or fragging, avoid splashing, and never boil or scrub rock with them attached.

corals.taxonomyNote: Mushrooms are sold at genus level as Discosoma; Discosoma nummiforme is used here as an accepted Indo-Pacific species.
corals.note: Smooth, flat discs in many colors that thrive in shaded spots.
corals.comments: Very hardy corallimorph that prefers low light and gentle flow. Spreads by budding and can crowd or shade neighboring corals over time.

corals.taxonomyNote: Hairy mushrooms are sold at genus level as Rhodactis; Rhodactis indosinensis is used here as a well-known accepted species.
corals.note: A fuzzy-textured mushroom that can fold up around food.
corals.comments: Hardy corallimorph that accepts small meaty foods. Can sting and overgrow nearby corals, so give it its own space.

corals.note: Bubbly, bright Caribbean mushrooms prized for their color combinations.
corals.comments: Corallimorph covered in short bubble-like tentacles. Prefers low to moderate light and gentle flow; benefits from occasional target feeding. Slower to spread than Discosoma.

corals.note: The classic clownfish host anemone, with bulb-tipped tentacles.
corals.comments: Add only to a mature, stable tank. Anemones wander until they find a spot they like and can sting corals along the way; cover pump and overflow intakes. Needs strong light plus occasional feeding of meaty foods.

inverts.notes: Sets up cleaning stations and picks parasites off fish. Sensitive to copper and to salinity swings; drip acclimate.
inverts.note: The red-and-white striped cleaner that will even pick at your fingers.
inverts.comments: Peaceful cleaner shrimp that also scavenges leftover food. Molts regularly; leave the shed shell for it to eat. Keep salinity stable and never dose copper.

inverts.notes: More reclusive than the skunk cleaner; provide caves. Sensitive to copper and to salinity swings; drip acclimate.
inverts.note: A deep red shrimp with white spots that stays close to caves.
inverts.comments: Peaceful cleaner shrimp that is shyer than Lysmata amboinensis and prefers shaded overhangs. Scavenges leftover food; never dose copper.

inverts.notes: Kept to eat Aiptasia pest anemones; results vary between individuals. Several look-alike Lysmata species are sold as peppermint shrimp.
inverts.note: A small striped shrimp famous for eating pest Aiptasia anemones.
inverts.comments: Peaceful scavenger that often eats Aiptasia. Well-fed individuals may ignore Aiptasia, and a rare few pick at zoanthids. Sensitive to copper.

inverts.notes: Leaves corals alone but fights other shrimp and may catch very small fish. Keep one, or a mated pair.
inverts.note: A long-armed, red-and-white banded shrimp with dramatic white antennae.
inverts.comments: Hardy boxer shrimp that scavenges and sometimes cleans fish. Territorial toward other shrimp, including its own kind unless paired.

inverts.notes: Grazes film algae and diatoms; can right itself if flipped, unlike many turbo and astraea snails. Sold at genus level as Trochus; Trochus histrio is used here as a well-known accepted species.
inverts.note: A cone-shaped grazing snail that keeps glass and rock clean.
inverts.comments: Hardy algae grazer that often breeds in aquariums. Does not need supplemental food while algae and biofilm are available.

inverts.notes: Grazes film and hair algae. Often cannot right itself if it falls onto its back; turn it over if you see it. Sold as Astraea tecta, a name WoRMS does not return as a marine record; Lithopoma tectum is the accepted name.
inverts.note: A pyramid-shaped grazer that works rock and glass all day.
inverts.comments: Hardy algae-grazing turban snail, a staple of reef cleanup crews. Keep a few per tank and add more only if algae outpaces them.

inverts.notes: Sold as Nassarius vibex; WoRMS lists Nassarius vibex (AphiaID 160401) as unaccepted, with Phrontis vibex accepted. Burrows in sand and eats leftover meaty food; needs a sand bed.
inverts.note: A sand-sifting scavenger that pops out of the sand when food lands.
inverts.comments: Scavenging snail that turns over the top of the sand bed and cleans up uneaten food. Needs a sand bed and does not graze algae.

inverts.notes: Grazes algae and scavenges, but may kill snails to take their shells. Provide spare empty shells.
inverts.note: A tiny hermit with bright blue legs that scours rock for algae.
inverts.comments: Small reef-safe hermit crab that eats algae and detritus. Offering a few empty shells one size up reduces fights and snail losses.

inverts.notes: Known for eating bubble algae. Most leave corals alone, but some large or underfed individuals pick at corals or small fish.
inverts.note: A green crab often added to eat bubble algae.
inverts.comments: Algae-eating crab that also scavenges. Feed occasionally if algae runs out to discourage it from picking at corals.

inverts.notes: A strong algae grazer that also eats coralline algae. It can carry or knock over loose frags, so glue frags down.
inverts.note: A small banded urchin that decorates itself with bits of shell and rubble.
inverts.comments: Algae-grazing urchin that stays small enough for mid-sized reef tanks. Sensitive to salinity changes; drip acclimate. Needs a steady supply of algae or supplemental seaweed.

inverts.notes: Mostly photosynthetic (hosts zooxanthellae in its mantle) with some filter feeding, so it needs strong light. Place on rock or sand where fish cannot pick at the mantle; some angelfish and wrasses will.
inverts.note: A giant clam with a vividly patterned mantle that opens toward the light.
inverts.comments: Needs a mature tank with strong lighting and stable calcium and alkalinity. Watch for pyramidellid snails that parasitize clams.

inverts.notes: Harmless to corals and fish but often starves in aquariums; needs a large, long-established tank with plenty of biofilm. Very sensitive to acclimation; drip acclimate slowly.
inverts.note: A striking cobalt-blue sea star that grazes biofilm on the rockwork.
inverts.comments: Grazes biofilm and detritus. Losses in the first months are common, so it suits only large, mature reefs. Do not expose it to air during acclimation.
